Relatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workers

Nepal-Tibet floods – latest updates

Visual guide: How the Nepal-Tibet flash flood unfolded

Nepali rescuers have built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue hundreds of trapped workers, as the death toll passed 1,000 nearly ⁠a week after devastating ​floods left a trail of destruction across the country’s towns and valleys.

About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts. The prime ⁠minister, Balendra Shah, said more than 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines had been restored in some areas.

“Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones and property,” Shah said.

Six days after the catastrophe struck the Himalayan border region, 4,400 people were still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist identification efforts.

In a statement posted to social media, Nepal police on Monday asked relatives of those missing to “provide a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the Nepal police hospital in Kathmandu, or the nearest district police office.

Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.

Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.

In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues .

At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.

Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims.

“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.”

She was waiting for her two other siblings, who live in the UK, to arrive on Tuesday so they could all try to get up to the village. She said she wanted to contact her grandmother or sister-in-law, who she thinks both survived the flood because their house is further up the mountain. Their village was still in a blackout, and making contact was impossible.

“I can’t go there; the situation is very bad,” she said. “I can’t go up there alone. I am not sure if we’ll be able to get them.”

The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse that sent a deluge of ice, rock and mud through Nepal’s border region with China , posing a massive challenge for the country’s six-month-old government.

The region is vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events such as intense monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.

In a late-night social media post, Shah said aid worth more than $42m had poured into the country, but that Nepalis were reeling. “The government understands the ​immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to ‌support them through this suffering and help ‌them return to normal life through rehabilitation,” the prime minister said.

Shah also said that 279 workers had so far been rescued from hydropower projects, where authorities estimated close to 1,000 people had been trapped. Days after the disaster, hope was rapidly diminisging that any of those trapped in a series of tunnels could be alive.

Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.

Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People’s Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side.

The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state broadcaster said on Monday.

Shah said the ​catastrophic event signalled the growing risks that the Himalayan region faces. “The region must therefore remain vigilant. The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change,” he wrote in his post.

stories.title: Trump tells FCC to punish journalist for calling his election results "mixed"
stories.summary: Trump furious at NBC's Kristen Welker for saying he had mixed results in primary endorsements.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Trump furious at NBC’s Kristen Welker for saying he had mixed results in primary endorsements.

President Trump yesterday demanded that the Federal Communications Commission punish or rebuke an NBC journalist for saying he has “mixed results” in his election endorsements. In the latest example of how Trump is using the FCC to harass reporters and news organizations that he dislikes, he said Meet the Press host Kristen Welker “will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment” for what he claimed was a “purposeful inaccuracy.”

“Kristen Welker, the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has ‘mixed results’ on his Endorsements of Candidates, when the recent WINS of Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei, stand at 100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House, recently and over the longterm. How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post .

A separate post from Trump yesterday said, “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT.” Trump also posted a rant on Friday about New York Times journalist Maggie Haberman, calling her “an unattractive person both inside and out” who “should be forced to turn over any and all money that she’s made through her fake reporting on me.” Trump referred to Haberman throughout his post as “Maggot Haberman.”

Trump’s post about Welker included an image purporting to show he has near-perfect results in his endorsements this year. “The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” Trump wrote.

Perhaps indicating that he will refer additional journalists for FCC punishment, Trump wrote that Welker “is not the only one. The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP.’”

Trump’s FCC chair has eagerly obeyed orders

The idea of the FCC punishing reporters for basic analysis of election results would have seemed far-fetched in previous administrations. The FCC website says the commission “cannot prevent the broadcast of any particular point of view,” and that it “generally will not intervene” in complaints about “one-sided news reports” because “it would be inconsistent with the First Amendment to replace the journalistic judgment of licensees with our own.”

Even during Trump’s first term, then-FCC Chairman Ajit Pai said that under the First Amendment, “the FCC does not have the authority to revoke a license of a broadcast station based on the content of a particular newscast.” Pai made the comment less than a week after Trump called on the FCC to revoke broadcast licenses from NBC and other networks for “fake news.”

An FCC investigation of Welker over an ordinary statement about election results seems much less far-fetched under Carr, who has embraced his role as Trump’s chief censor. Carr has made it clear he takes orders from Trump , abandoning his previous position—which he held under Democratic presidents —that the FCC must operate independently of White House interference.

Welker said in an appearance on NBC 4 Washington that Trump “has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries” and that “he’s had some mixed results but most recently his pick of Senator Darline Graham, of course the sister of the late Senator Lindsay Graham, was successful in her primary battle.” Trump’s post attacking Welker claimed that “the story of [Graham’s] Victory was hardly covered by anybody,” despite Welker mentioning it in the very statement that triggered Trump’s wrath.

Poynter Senior Media Writer Tom Jones writes , “What Welker said about Trump’s endorsements having mixed results was true. Trump just didn’t like it.” While Trump praised himself for his successful endorsements, he didn’t mention primary losses by Republican gubernatorial candidates Burt Jones in Georgia and Randy Feenstra in Iowa and the failed re-election bid by Rep. Cory Mills (R-Florida).

Carr uses news-distortion policy to threaten networks

An NBC News spokesperson told several media outlets that “Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her.” We contacted NBC News and will update this article if it has any further comment.

Welker is hardly the first TV journalist to discuss Trump’s mixed endorsement results. “Already, just this month alone, six of the president’s endorsed candidates have lost their races, and so there are questions about the power of his endorsements,” CNN White House correspondent Alayna Treene said on Inside Politics .

In June, Trump abruptly ended an interview with Welker after she challenged his claims of election rigging in California. Trump stated that “all I have to do is look” when Welker asked him for evidence of cheating. “That’s not evidence,” Welker responded.

If Carr does investigate Welker, he could do so under the FCC’s news distortion policy. Carr has repeatedly invoked the rarely enforced news distortion policy and a rule against broadcast hoaxes in various threats to Trump’s perceived enemies in the media. We asked the FCC chairman’s office today if the commission will investigate Welker and will update this article if we get a response.

Previous FCC leaders set such a high bar for proving news distortion that the policy was all but abandoned until Carr made it a focal point of his attempts to punish broadcasters. In September 2025, Carr threatened to revoke ABC station licenses for news distortion if they continued airing Jimmy Kimmel’s show.

Trump and FCC try to reshape the media

While Carr can cause trouble for licensed broadcasters and networks simply by issuing threats, he went far beyond mere threats in the case of ABC. The Carr FCC ordered ABC to file early license-renewal applications for the eight TV stations it owns and operates and justified the proceeding by accusing ABC of violating anti-discrimination rules with diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices.

ABC owner Disney is fighting back with a lawsuit against Carr and the FCC , saying it has faced a campaign of censorship in retaliation for the protected speech of its journalists and network programs. Both conservative and liberal groups have urged the FCC to back off.

The Trump administration has also sought to reshape the media through merger approvals. Paramount won FCC approval to buy Skydance after agreeing to install what Carr called a “bias monitor” at CBS. Paramount later won Justice Department approval to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, months after CEO David Ellison reportedly told Trump administration officials that he would make big changes at the Warner-owned CNN.

In March, Trump and Carr demanded more positive media coverage of the Iran war, with Carr claiming without evidence that broadcasters aired “hoaxes and news distortions.” Last year, Carr accused Comcast of news distortion when its subsidiary NBC refused to adopt the Trump administration narrative on the deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the commission’s only Democrat, responded to Trump’s latest threat yesterday. “As I’ve said many times, the FCC has no authority to punish journalists this administration doesn’t like,” Gomez wrote . “These threats to press freedom are dangerous. They undermine the foundation of our democracy, and they have no place in it.”

stories.title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Andrew Bailey warns G20
stories.summary: The governor of the Bank of England warned of AI's “volatility” caused by energy shocks from the US-Iran war.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 31 August 2026

The governor of the Bank of England has warned G20 finance ministers that artificial intelligence could cause a global economic downturn and pose a significant cyber security risk to financial systems.

Andrew Bailey said any collapse of growth in the AI sector could lead to a "future market correction" that spreads worldwide.

In an open letter to finance ministers in the US on Monday, he said companies around the world should prepare for security breaches "involving simultaneous disruption across multiple firms".

Earlier this month, a group of 100 firms , including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, urged countries and groups to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.

Bailey told the G20 finance ministers that a combination of highly priced stock markets, increased borrowing by investors, and the growing concentration of money into a small number of major technology companies could amplify any future market correction.

"The issue is not simply that investors are borrowing more, but that leverage is interacting with high valuations and market concentration, in particular the increasing cross-investment between artificial intelligence (AI) companies and hyper scalers, in a way that could amplify a future market correction," he said.

Bailey has called on those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis".

Bailey, who was writing in his capacity as chairman of the Financial Stability Board international watchdog (FSB), expressed concern about the "volatility" prompted by the effect of energy supply shocks caused by the US-Iran war.

His warning comes as the UK government is seeking to grow the country's "sovereign AI" capacity, developing homegrown AI technology to ensure the UK is not dependent on services from abroad.

Ministers want to see companies compete for the funding to help tackle challenges like cutting waiting lists in the NHS and bolstering cybersecurity and defence.

But there is growing concern that AI companies are increasingly developing models that can easily override the safeguarding systems of banks and financial centres.

Andrew Bailey wants those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release"

This summer has seen OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all reveal their AI tools doing things they should not, with some AI agents going so far as to impersonate real people in order to get past security hurdles.

The FSB which Bailey leads is a global watchdog which monitors finance ministry officials, banks and securities regulators. It includes officials from the US, UK, France, Germany, Canada, Japan, Australia, China and Saudi Arabia.

stories.body:
Japan’s collision with Donald Trump reveals the dilemma facing Britain: economic independence is becoming more necessary – and more tricky to achieve

“I n the midst of every crisis lies great opportunity” is an aphorism attributed to Albert Einstein . It seems to be taken to heart by this White House. A global bond sell-off sparked by an inflationary shock emanating from the Gulf sees Donald Trump seeking to restrict plans by Japan – a longtime ally – to reduce dependence on an international system America dominates.

Japan, a successful exporter, has long done things its own way. For years Tokyo saw off the bond vigilantes despite running enormous deficits and a huge national debt. It demonstrated how a central bank could fund public spending and keep interest rates low if it wanted to. This economic model was refined by Shinzo Abe, Japan’s longest-serving prime minister. However, this week the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent , called time on Abenomics as his price for US help in stabilising Japan’s currency. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi, he indicated, should shrink her $2tn spending plans and raise rates. Abenomics did not suddenly become financially impossible. It became inconvenient to the issuer of the world’s reserve currency.

Kevin Warsh, Mr Trump’s handpicked chair of the US Federal Reserve, has made it clear that he will raise interest rates in response to inflationary pressures. Others will be expected to follow. In Japan’s case, Washington fears that a yen crisis could become a bond crisis. A disorderly rout could force Japan into ever larger currency interventions – and repeated appeals to Washington to help defend the yen. If such aid proved inadequate, Tokyo could end up defending its currency by dumping US treasury bonds – of which it has more than a trillion dollars worth – and put upward pressure on the very yields Mr Bessent is trying to contain. His demand that Tokyo raise rates and cut spending is not just about Japanese inflation. It is about trying to prevent Tokyo’s adjustment to the Iran shock being exported on to America’s balance sheet.

Mr Burnham’s first Commons speech as prime minister suggests an expansive programme to raise living standards and get growth through regional reindustrialisation. This, he says, rests on the “bedrock” of fiscal responsibility. Mr Burnham promises an activist state to deal with four decades of underinvestment and privatisation. But retaining Rachel Reeves’s fiscal framework leaves his investment plans hostage to interest rates, debt costs and feverish “ headroom ” speculation. Turmoil in global bond markets could derail his industrial strategy before it gets going.

Japan’s big bazooka spending programme was meant to do what Mr Burnham now says Britain must do on a smaller scale: use the state to rebuild productive capacity , reduce strategic dependence and build its export competitiveness. Tokyo has the fiscal firepower, a central bank able to dominate the sovereign bond market and trillions invested overseas. The UK government could mimic that and change its fiscal rules, its relationship to the Bank of England and the way investment is accounted for.

But Japan is Mr Burnham’s problem writ large. The war in Iran made it urgent to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. But the conflict’s inflationary shock makes that objective harder – though not impossible – to pursue. Mr Trump’s team is using its leverage over the yen to restrain Tokyo’s plan to make Japan resilient to external price spikes. Mr Burnham has been forewarned: the Gulf inflation shock wave bolsters the argument for economic independence while making the means of achieving it more difficult.

stories.title: Spaces in male prisons fall to lowest level of year, sources say
stories.summary: Jails in England and Wales are nearing maximum capacity as the justice secretary prepares to give more details in the Commons on the early-release scheme to free inmates.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The early release scheme was launched in September to tackle overcrowding

Published 3 hours ago

The number of available spaces across the male prison estate in England and Wales has fallen to its lowest this year, sources have told the BBC.

As of 1 September, there were about 1,500 free spaces, just under half the number available at the start of June, which Ministry of Justice (MoJ) figures put at 3,040.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris is due to give more details in the Commons later on changes to the early-release scheme, which aims to free up space in prisons as they near maximum capacity.

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced changes to the scheme, which will mean more prisoners, including those convicted of manslaughter, will remain behind bars for longer.

Laundry rooms to be turned into cells to tackle prison overcrowding Published 7 hours ago

MoJ figures show the number of available male prison spaces has been steadily falling since the middle of June, with the last official figures released on 24 August placing them at 1,665.

This week's numbers have not been officially released due to Monday's bank holiday but prison sources say vacancies have fallen once again.

The government has said it would create more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.

An investment of £110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the MoJ said.

The justice secretary told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.

Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly.

"This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."

Norris said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

But the chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."

Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity.

Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being let out of prison in tranches from October.

On Sunday, the prime minister told BBC Breakfast anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.

Extra prison space would also be created by deporting more foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.

Government figures show there were 10,134 foreign nationals held in custody on 30 June, 3,283 of whom were on remand and would not be eligible for deportation.

In the year to June, 5,962 foreign offenders were sent back to their home countries - the highest rate of deportations since 2017 and a 12% increase on the previous year.

stories.title: Meta accepts U.S. safety rules while pitching softer tools abroad
stories.summary: As governments consider banning social media for under-16s, Meta is turning to influencers to argue that parental controls are a better solution.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tech Giants

As governments consider banning social media for under-16s, Meta is turning to influencers to argue that parental controls are a better solution.

In June, Indian actor Hiten Tejwani told his 732,000 followers that “Instagram is okay” in a reel promoting Meta’s Teen Accounts. Ironically, Tejwani had barred his 17-year-old twin son and daughter from using social media until they turned 16.

The reel was made after a Zoom call with Meta representatives, who explained what their campaign endorsed. Teen Accounts, launched in 2024, gives 13- to 16-year-olds private accounts, screen-time limits, and age-appropriate content. Tejwani, who was paid for the campaign but did not disclose the amount, told Rest of World that he agreed to participate because he saw it as an effort to inform parents rather than encourage every child to join social media.

There has been a global rise in the number of such reels in recent months, as Meta pursues influencer campaigns promoting Teen Accounts, particularly in countries that are mulling a social media ban for children under 16, according to a recent report by Tech Transparency Project, a Washington-based research organization.

Meta is using parent influencers to both soften its image and fight back against the existential threat of social media bans for kids under 16, Katie Paul, director of Tech Transparency Project, told Rest of World .

The campaign comes at a time when Meta is facing heat in the U.S. over child safety concerns. On August 26, the company settled a major trial in the U.S., agreeing to make several safety limitations the default option for teens. Australia, Brazil, and Indonesia have already banned social media for kids under 16. At least 22 other countries are reportedly designing and proposing similar policies .

“If countries around the world follow the lead of Australia and enact these bans, Meta will be cut off from young people who are essential to its growth plans,” Paul said.

Meta’s campaign against social media restrictions

Tech Transparency Project found that Meta has been pushing a narrative of safety through “momfluencers” across the world, from India to Canada to Indonesia.

While the campaign plays out slightly differently in each country, the fundamental strategy is this: Meta pays Instagram influencer parents or celebrities with large followings — and in some cases, child safety groups — to promote Teen Accounts, Paul said. A teen account on Facebook or Instagram allows parents to supervise content and communication for under-16s.

“The underlying message is that Meta is capable of self-regulating child safety protection and that bans are unnecessary,” Paul said. “Some of these influencers have hundreds of thousands and even millions of followers, making them a potent tool for Meta’s corporate messaging.”

Meta has also hosted several “screen smart” events across the world, including in the U.S., New Zealand, Malaysia, and the Philippines, to promote teen safety and parental supervision. In Australia, it sponsored a youth mental health service conducting “ safety camps .” In Indonesia, Meta commissioned a survey , which revealed “overwhelming” parental support for teen accounts with safety features.

Influencing controls

Age verification tools are less than ideal, but they’re still better than outright bans, David Greene, senior counsel at nonprofit digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation, told Rest of World .

“Mandated age limits are designed to deny young people their fundamental human rights — to access information, arts, and culture, to form communities, to speak, and to play,” Greene said. “Age estimation technology threatens all users’ privacy by collecting people’s sensitive, personal information, exposing them to risk of data breaches and government data demands, and chilling speech on sensitive issues.”

Parental tools and youth accounts are a better option than bans, he said. There is probably a role for broader-based social media literacy education as well, “whether that happens through influencers, the government, parents, or peers.”

Snehaalata Shah, an Indian parenting and travel blogger, was approached by an agency for the Teen Accounts campaign. She did not wish to disclose the name of the agency. This was her first paid campaign for Meta.

“They gave us a brief idea where I have to inculcate the teen account features in the middle of the script,” she told Rest of World . “I made a script, and a little bit of changes were done by the agency.” The teen account for her 14-year-old daughter lets Shah keep track of follow and direct message requests and screen time.

“The main takeaway for parents is that there are tools and safeguards available to make social media more age-appropriate for teenagers and to give parents more control and reassurance,” Sonam Jaggi, who runs the account @momavengers with 322,000 followers, told Rest of World . The promo shot by the mom of two kids — 8 and 1 — has amassed 310 million views , and more than half a million likes.

A November 2025 report by a Meta whistleblower and several online kids safety organizations evaluated 47 out of 53 safety features for teens. It found that 64% of the features were broken, missing, or ineffective.

Shah posted a promo reel for Teen Accounts for her 238,000 followers on July 7 — coincidentally the same day Meta published a statement claiming it had “ zero-tolerance ” for child sexual abuse material, and that it had taken down more than 160,000 accounts.

“If every country bans Instagram or Facebook under 16, of course, there would be loss to [Meta],” Shah told Rest of World. She said she recognized there may be a business motive driving these ads. But given that her 6-year-old son knows how to switch accounts on YouTube instead of logging off when the child time restriction notification pops up, she would still promote the tools to protect her teen.

Tejwani, too, is standing by his decision, but as a parent. Although it was a paid campaign to begin with, his heart is in it, and he’s still happy to entertain questions from other parents and media.

“It is compensation we have to charge, definitely. But otherwise, if I’m talking about it right now, if somebody’s asking me otherwise, this is not a paid thing. I will definitely inform everyone,” Tejwani told Rest of World .

Why the global push to break free from Big Tech keeps falling short

In this excerpt from the book “The Rulers: Corporate Power in the Age of AI and the Cloud,” writer Cecilia Rikap examines how Europe, India, Brazil, and China are taking on big tech companies.

AI safety is designed in the West, and failing users everywhere

Visa restrictions are deterring international AI talent from building companies in the U.S., giving other nations including China an opportunity to catch up.

stories.body:
From ceramic goblin feet to furry disembodied legs, Korean-Chinese artist Woo Jin Joo is using London junk to inject the art world with a spirit of playfulness

W oo Jin Joo’s studio is full of magic. Ceramic green goblin feet line the windowsill, disembodied furry legs jut out of one white wall and, on the table behind where the Korean-Chinese artist sits drinking tea, a headless being dressed in a black coat squats, arms aloft in warning.

There are also neat racks of colourful thread next to a freehand embroidery machine, the source of this supernatural hoard. This is where Joo creates much of her art – surface embroideries and sculptural 3D creatures inspired by Korean myth, philosophy and the relationship between humans and the natural world.

“When I use the embroidery machine I feel like I’m painting,” she says. “It’s as if each thread has its own life.”

Joo was born and raised in Korea – mainly by her grandmother – before moving to the UK 12 years ago to study at Central Saint Martins and then the Royal Academy in London. Swapping east Asia for west Europe started her thinking about how she was shaped by culture and the world around her. “That transition made me want to explore who I am and how I see things.”

In 2021 she worked out how she wanted to go about it. She embroidered the 10 Daoist symbols of longevity, typically used to wish someone long life, on to an old Ikea bag – a plastic product that could take up to 1,000 years to decompose.

“It was that work that made me feel a connection, a way of drawing ideas together to make a transformation that resonated with religious beliefs as well as myth,” she says.

Guided by the idea from Korean folklore and shamanism that inanimate objects can become spirited beings called dokkaebi , she looked at the junk discarded in London with fresh eyes. Now she often uses found objects in her work – a creature with many feet peers out of an old shirt sleeve; a discarded wooden side-table now sprouts a 5ft-tall dokkaebi leg. “I love the idea that the small and mundane have spirit,” she explains. “We need to realise that the ordinary is special.”

Joo is part of a new wave of creatives showing that traditional, sometimes archaic, craft can be used to make very modern, joyful work. Makers are not just keeping these skills alive but evolving how they can be used. “I think a lot of makers are very experimental now, craft is no longer just about material knowledge, but about experimenting and playfulness. This means more people are drawn to it,” says Joo.

She is preparing for her first solo show, Bodily Inbetweenness, at London’s Ruup & Form gallery, which opens during Shoreditch Design Week. For this, she explores a new type of spirit, human emotions and how we display them – a concept that Joo shows through powerful figures, slightly reminiscent of corn dollies but 5ft tall, poking out of the walls. “For me, a sense of fun always wants to come out, but for some people it’s awkward, it doesn’t fully emerge,” she says.

The first sculpture in this series – I Hear Things Existing With Me, a contemplative figure slightly sunken into the wall it leans on – was one of the standout pieces at London’s Collect Craft Fair in February. Collect’s director, TF Chan, believes that you never forget the first time you see Joo’s work.

after newsletter promotion

“Mine was a pair of ceramic legs with each toe tipped in glossy red nail varnish,” he says. “In my view, she embodies the values of contemporary craft: closely bound to the artist’s heritage while accommodating both serious intellectual engagement and sheer delight.”

Joo loves the widespread interest in Korean culture – currently encompassing everything from pop to skincare and it is perhaps one of the reasons her work feels so current. “Because I’m from Chinese as well as Korean heritage it’s been very meaningful to see both cultures celebrated. I think that international attention has meant that, especially within Korea, there’s now more interest in preserving and honouring traditions.”

For Joo, seeing herself as a maker as well as an artist is a point of pride at a time when craftspeople continue to struggle for art world acceptance. “There is still a hierarchy,” she says. “A lot of fine artists now use craft like ceramic or textiles and that’s seen as part of their knowledge. Whereas if you come from a craft background what you do is rarely considered fine art. It should be free-flowing.”

With another show to prepare for at the Harley Foundation, Nottinghamshire, later this year, Joo has long hours ahead of her in the studio creating her magical creatures, but she relishes that. “I think it’s the trickle of everydayness that really shapes who I am and how I see things. That really is what my work is about.”

stories.title: Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM
stories.summary: The prime minister's first appearance in Parliament comes more than six weeks after he entered No 10.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 hour ago

Andy Burnham has taken questions from MPs in the House of Commons for the first time since taking over as prime minister.

The statement on his future plans for power comes six weeks after he took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July, just before Parliament's summer recess.

Here are the main points from what he said.

He plans to give away power

Burnham told MPs his time as mayor of Greater Manchester had given him a "clear theory of growth" that further devolution of power away from Westminster would help boost the UK's economic prospects.

But he said he wanted to avoid a "two-tier England" - where areas that have already been given greater powers pull away from those that have not.

He announced that work was under way with Cornwall council and its six MPs on a devolution deal, "with or without" an elected mayor, to help the rural economy.

Burnham's move to grant the county greater powers, without requiring it to team up with councils in neighbouring areas, could open the door to more devolution for other single counties.

Burnham also said he would meet leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to explore more local powers there.

He was pressed on defence spending

The statement was the first chance for Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to grill Burnham on defence spending following headlines on the issue over the summer.

Chancellor John Healey was appointed by Burnham after quitting as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer , calling for the UK to spend 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2030.

However, since entering the Treasury, Healey is yet to attach a date to this spending target, and has faced pressure to do so in recent days.

Healey has said a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP will be set out at the next government spending review, expected in spring next year.

But in a potential signal of his intentions in this area, Burham said the arguments Healey had made about defence spending in his former role were a key reason why he had put him in charge of the Treasury.

Andy Burnham chaired his first Number 10 North meeting in July

He will go to the UN's climate summit

Burnham confirmed he would attend the COP31 climate summit in November, as he vowed to "meet the climate challenge".

The annual UN climate change conference will take place in Antalya, Turkey, allowing Burnham to come face to face with many world leaders and senior officials.

While Sir Keir attended COP summits when he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak was criticised in 2022 for not going because he had "other pressing domestic commitments".

Burnham's pledge to attend the summit comes as he faces a looming decision about whether to allow drilling to start in the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield, in the North Sea, which have been in legal limbo for a year.

He wants to continue leasehold reform

Labour's 2024 election manifesto promised to "finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end", after campaigners said it was unfair that flat owners had little control over spiralling property costs.

A draft Leasehold and Commonhold Reform Bill published by Starmer's government earlier this year included plans to cap ground rent at £250, ban the sale of new leasehold flats and give homeowners greater control over how their buildings are managed.

Under the bill, leasehold would be banned "except in limited cases", and developers would no longer be allowed to sell new flats as leasehold.

That bill is yet to be introduced to Parliament, but Burnham confirmed he intended to "bring forward" a Commonhold and Leasehold Bill during the current session of Parliament, which began in May and would normally last around a year.

He paid tribute to Starmer

Burnham kicked off his Commons statement by paying tribute to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, who had announced he was resigning as MP for Holborn and St Pancras just hours earlier.

Sir Keir had given the UK "a lifetime of service", Burnham said, including delivering the Hillsborough Law which demands more accountability from public officials during official inquiries, as well as work to achieve peace in Ukraine.

He also praised Sir Keir for leading Labour to one of its "best victories" in the 2024 election.

He said Sir Keir had "created a platform to change this country for the better" which the new government would "use well".

stories.title: Trump admin shelves Cyclospora research despite record-breaking outbreak
stories.summary: The CDC has tallied nearly 30,000 confirmed and probable cases this summer.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The CDC has tallied nearly 30,000 confirmed and probable cases this summer.

The Trump administration is halting vital federal research on the foodborne parasite Cyclospora, despite the record-breaking, nationwide outbreak of the diarrheal pathogen, according to Politico .

Of the three research programs that represent nearly all of the Cyclospora work at the US Department of Agriculture, two have been defunded, and the third is about to lose every scientist working on it. The Trump administration is shuttering the USDA’s Beltsville Agricultural Research Center near Washington, DC, and moving its work to a location in Iowa. That includes relocating the remaining Cyclospora research.

Although the research is still funded, insiders told Politico that not one of the scientists working on the project plans to relocate from Maryland to Iowa. Instead, they are either retiring, being reassigned to a different project, or leaving the USDA’s research services.

“They will have no parasitologists,” one USDA employee told Politico. “There will be a big knowledge gap.”

The US is experiencing the largest Cyclospora outbreak ever recorded. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has tallied nearly 30,000 confirmed and probable cases this summer. At least 922 people have been hospitalized with cyclosporiasis, and two have died. Since 2018, the US has generally reported between 2,000 and 5,000 cases, though the US reported 1,180 cases in 2025.

Lost research opportunities

Cyclospora is difficult to work with in a laboratory compared to other foodborne pathogens, such as E. coli or Salmonella. Cyclospora grow and reproduce only in the human gut, not in lab conditions. Although the parasite can be isolated from feces in labs, it can sometimes be difficult to fish out; it can be shed intermittently or at low levels, requiring repeat fecal samples from an infected person. The parasite is also harder to study using genetic techniques. It has a much larger genome than bacteria, making genomic sequencing costlier and more laborious. It also reproduces sexually, meaning each generation will have new mixes of genes, making it harder to trace back lineages of the parasite to a single contaminated food. That’s in contrast to bacteria, which reproduce asexually, creating clones that are often nearly identical and easy to trace.

With this year’s outbreak, researchers hoped for a surge in understanding of the parasite. “We see this as an enormous opportunity, this current outbreak, to have really a lot of samples that could help us understand these outbreaks better,” another USDA employee told Politico. However, people who worked on the defunded Cyclospora programs are barred from doing any more research and are simply preserving samples they already had from previous outbreaks.

While funding may be restored at a later time, experts said the disruption to the research will be difficult to overcome. “The bigger impact is that there are very few people in the world that study these [parasites],” Joelle Mosso, associate vice president for science growers at the Western Growers Association, a trade group representing produce farmers, told Politico. “It’s not just replacing the lab. It takes decades to build expertise.”

stories.title: EFF to Courts: Don’t Rewrite Copyright Over AI Hype
stories.summary: The history of technology is rife with copyright panics. In the 1980s, major rightsholders ran to Congress and the courts, claiming that videotape recorders (VTR) were “to the American film producer and the American public as the Boston strangler is to the woman home alone .” Then, the Supreme Court declined to embrace the hype, noting that the VTR was capable of all kinds of non-infringing uses, like time-shifting and cautioning courts to avoid rewriting copyright law in response to new technologies. We believe that courts now should be similarly wary about the hype surrounding AI. Hollywood’s hyperbole has echoed that of composer John Phillip Sousa , who claimed in 1906 that the player piano and the gramophone would destroy music composition; portrait artists who feared the camera would replace the paintbrush. None of these things happened. Cameras, for example, sparked a resurgence of portraiture and, by making it possible for more people to create images, led to unexpected developments—like the rise of photojournalism. New markets, new ideas, and new creators are actually what copyright is supposed to promote, not restrict. Using copyright to lock in existing gatekeepers and massive rightsholders’ profits helps neither the public nor individual artists. Generative AI has sparked the latest wave of anxiety and with it a massive wave of litigation. In multiple cases around the U.S. and the world, rightsholders are asking courts to do precisely what the Supreme Court warned against: dramatically expand copyright protections based in substantial part on hyperbole and speculation. They should decline to do so. Copyright owners claim that unless courts abandon 300-year-old copyright principles—and give rightsholders the power to control non-infringing works created by others—an imagined flood of AI-generated works will devastate creative markets. stories.body:
Canadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insults

US politics live – latest updates

Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada.

Days before Canada is due to retaliate against Trump’s sweeping tariffs with its own duties on US goods, the Canadian prime minister criticized US officials for insulting his country. “It is beneath their office,” he said.

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions” about trade, Carney said.

Trump signed an executive order last week directing the US federal government to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America – a move that has been rejected by Canadians.

The US president’s most senior trade negotiator has meanwhile downplayed the potentially disastrous effects of a US trade war with Canada, declaring the spat to be “more their emergency than ours”.

The US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, argued that Canada was more vulnerable after the breakdown in talks set the stage for sweeping tariffs between the two neighbors, telling Politico: “There are no negotiations happening on trade right now.”

The comment comes just more than a week after US-Canada trade talks imploded. The US levied 50% tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods.

Canada, the US’s second-largest trading partner , announced it would impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of American goods starting on 8 September. Now, US residents are poised to feel extreme pressure from Trump’s tariffs and Canada’s retaliatory measures, including on day-to-day items.

Greer appeared to blame the escalating trade war on Canadian officials, telling Politico: “It’s not clear Canada wants a deal.

“If Canada believes that prohibiting and banning American goods and services is appropriate, then obviously that’s something that the United States should consider as well.”

Unacceptable asks from Canada included lighter taxes on heavy-duty trucks, according to Greer, who said such requests torpedoed the trade talks.

Canadian officials, on the other hand, attributed the collapsed negotiations to a White House disagreement over who was directing trade talks. Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, also said that American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant”, but added: “In Quebec, these are rights.”

Trump, for his part, has argued in recent weeks that Canada “wants the benefits” of being a US state, without being one – a preoccupation of the US president – as he lashed out at the country’s leaders. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” claimed Trump. “No more!!!”

Greer suggested that negotiations broke down after a misunderstanding around what was, and wasn’t, on the table. “Was that political? I don’t know,” he told Politico. “Was it economic? … I’m not sure how much economic sense it makes because the choice is not between the current tariffs and … you know, duty-free trade. Like, that is that. Those weren’t the options.”

stories.title: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
stories.summary: Japanese companies are doubling down on India amid a shrinking domestic market and rising risks in China.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Brands like Uniqlo and Muji have rapidly expanded in India

Published 31 August 2026

India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent.

If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India.

Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding.

Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson , external is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai.

It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets.

MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector.

Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake.

Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific.

More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report , external . GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs.

"Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200m fund in India, told the BBC.

Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments in India through some 120 agreements during PM Sanae Takaichi's visit in July

At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says.

"Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited."

Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth.

Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago.

After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.

But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle.

At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments. They signed around 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. In fact, Goyal has said Japan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country.

Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal.

Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India.

The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently , external , is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India".

But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC.

India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says.

"With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides."

India's consumer market is growing fast as discretionary incomes rise

For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time.

India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai.

But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts.

"Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll , external .

"Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China."

Also, India remains a tough country to do business.

Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese.

An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed , external .

Chinese state media , external was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts.

It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere.

stories.title: Autonomous weapons can select targets without human help – now is the time for binding rules
stories.summary: One-way military drones already have the capability to select their targets. Anelo/Shutterstock Government experts are meeting in Geneva, Switzerland, to work towards a possible negotiating mandate on autonomous weapons systems (AWS). These are military systems that can select and engage targets without human intervention. This major international gathering follows a recent call by the UN and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) for urgent controls on these weapons , sometimes dubbed “killer robots” in descriptions by the media . Recent events in Ukraine have further consolidated concerns that a slide towards weapons with full autonomy (and without meaningful human control) is well underway. According to the New York Times, a Russian drone attacked a petrol station in Zaporizhzhia on July 6, killing three civilians. What marked it out was the drone’s use of AI to decide where and when to strike. The drone aircraft had been programmed to fly towards the petrol station. But on its approach, an AI system autonomously chose the precise target – probably propane tanks – based on its ability to recognise them. On August 25, Mirjana Spoljaric, the president of the ICRC, and António Guterres, the secretary-general of the United Nations, issued their joint appeal to the international community to agree on legally binding rules regulating the development and use of AWS. New technologies are making it cheaper and easier for nations to put together these weapons. Thus, the UN and ICRC appeal for binding rules could not be more urgent. stories.body:
Government experts are meeting in Geneva, Switzerland, to work towards a possible negotiating mandate on autonomous weapons systems (AWS). These are military systems that can select and engage targets without human intervention.

This major international gathering follows a recent call by the UN and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) for urgent controls on these weapons , sometimes dubbed “killer robots” in descriptions by the media .

Recent events in Ukraine have further consolidated concerns that a slide towards weapons with full autonomy (and without meaningful human control) is well underway. According to the New York Times, a Russian drone attacked a petrol station in Zaporizhzhia on July 6, killing three civilians. What marked it out was the drone’s use of AI to decide where and when to strike.

The drone aircraft had been programmed to fly towards the petrol station. But on its approach, an AI system autonomously chose the precise target – probably propane tanks – based on its ability to recognise them.

On August 25, Mirjana Spoljaric, the president of the ICRC, and António Guterres, the secretary-general of the United Nations, issued their joint appeal to the international community to agree on legally binding rules regulating the development and use of AWS.

New technologies are making it cheaper and easier for nations to put together these weapons. Thus, the UN and ICRC appeal for binding rules could not be more urgent. The international community is ideally placed to start negotiations soon, building on many years of diplomatic talks.

For the past decade, governments have debated how AWS challenge existing international law and what should be done under the auspices of the convention on certain conventional weapons, a UN arms control framework. Since 2017, the group of governmental experts (GGE) on lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) – which is part of the convention on certain conventional weapons – has convened typically twice a year.

The experts are meeting again this week in Geneva. The aim is to agree a governance framework and language for a rolling text that could be the foundation for negotiations. This text provides a baseline for continued discussions in November.

While this process has been rife with political disagreements, most experts agree on the need to retain some level of meaningful human control over the use of autonomous systems.

Moral significance

This demonstrates a shared sense by states participating in the process that human judgment is pivotal for the laws governing warfare. It also shows that the moral significance of warfare underlines the importance of human responsibility.

Human judgment is also embedded in international humanitarian law. Targeting processes require context-specific judgments about the targets themselves, potential harm to civilians from striking the target and other precautions. These tasks cannot be delegated to machines.

AI-enabled systems show how technology already shapes human perceptions of targets and risk. With autonomous weapons, the system shifts from influencing human judgement to exercising the targeting function itself.

Any AI system is only as good as the data it has been trained on, or that it works with. For armed conflicts, this data is difficult to come by and is almost always insufficient for dynamic and variable human contexts. This means many systems are likely to be technically inadequate.

The problem becomes quite visible with rules around assessing proportionality, for example, which is a context specific judgement about anticipated civilian harm versus military advantage.

Militaries may try to quantify targeting decisions in a way that creates the appearance of precision. However, the underlying legal judgment remains qualitative regardless. Technical accuracy, therefore, is not the same as lawfulness or moral consideration .

Only humans can understand the significance of respecting the inherent rights and dignity of other humans. Decisions to end human life must therefore be made qualitatively, by humans, in order to be morally and legally justifiable. Without this provision, and clear guidelines around it, we argue that governments risk running into a legal vacuum and a steep moral abyss .

AWS, especially those that prioritise speed and scale of action though AI, carry a significant risk of enabling an uncontrolled and rapid escalation. Escalation from crisis to war, or from conflict to a higher level of violence, could come about by erroneous indications of attack or by a simple sensor or computer error.

Unpredictable systems could give leaders false impressions of the capabilities of those systems. This could lead to overconfidence or encourage preemptive attacks.

Inevitable outcome?

One argument raised by academic researchers in the context of AWS is that they become necessary because they are inevitable. The risk is that more countries opt for full autonomy as components become cheaper and readily available, exacerbating an arms race.

However, an adversary’s conduct does not release a state from its own obligations under international humanitarian law. Following those rules is also part of what makes military force legitimate , including through civilian protection, precautions and accountability. We might turn the argument around and say: legally binding rules become inevitable, because they are absolutely necessary.

Governments and advocacy groups have worked hard over the past decade to put together a lucid proposal for the regulation of AWS. Some efforts are intended to prohibit those systems that target humans directly, or that are unpredictable and therefore cannot be meaningfully controlled by a human. All other AWS must be strictly regulated.

There are signs of political momentum. In November 2025, 156 states voted in favour of a UN General Assembly resolution that “draws attention to the serious challenges and concerns” that autonomous weapons raise. A legally binding instrument is possible, even if some states resist it.

The time is now. Clear, binding rules would help ensure that increasingly autonomous warfare does not make violence easier to unleash and harder to control.

stories.body:
When Washington unveiled its economic “D-Day” on August 19, the latest tightening of the financial siege and the blockade around Iran’s ports, it believed it was applying decisive leverage. But in Tehran the move was read as something else entirely – as confirmation that the US still prefers pressure to any settlement it might one day have to honour.

Across a political system that agrees on almost nothing, the interpretation was remarkably uniform. The economic stabilisers around the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, saw the US as reneging on a deal, while Ahmad Vahidi’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commanders saw their own warnings about American perfidy vindicated.

So whatever faith remained in Iran about US willingness to close a deal has thinned further. That erosion of trust now shapes what Tehran will and will not accept.

It is important to realise that Iran is making existential decisions about the survival strategy of the Islamic Republic itself. The old vocabulary of reformist against principlist – or moderate against hardliner – no longer reflects the real struggle inside the system.

The contest that matters runs between those who believe the Islamic Republic survives best by converting its wartime leverage into economic and diplomatic gains and those who believe survival depends instead on permanent confrontation. Both camps are loyal to the regime, and both argue in good faith about how to keep it alive. That makes the debate far harder to resolve.

It is also a debate with no single arbiter, because Iran today is best understood as a network state. Power runs through a decentralised structure that is horizontal in the way it is organised. The vertical hierarchy once associated with the former supreme leader Ali Khamenei has quietly dissolved.

His son Mojtaba Khamenei sits at the formal apex and shapes outcomes largely through appointments. He has installed Mohsen Rezaee , a founder member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as his representative on the supreme national security council. He is also rebuilding the Bayt – the office of the supreme leader that has long been the system’s true centre of gravity – around loyalists such as his new chief of staff, Mahdi Khamoushi .

Yet Mojtaba rules as a balancer rather than a decider, careful never to let any one node or hub dominate the system. Beneath him, authority is spread across the nodes of the security establishment. Rezaee coordinates strategy from the council, while Vahidi commands the military muscle, from the missile force to the naval pressure in the Strait of Hormuz.

Parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf , brokers the relationship between parliament and the security men. Pezeshkian’s government shoulders the economy, and the foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, handles the messages abroad. No single figure combines all of these functions in one pair of hands.

Iran’s shifting power balance

But this horizontal picture is shifting, because the war has centralised power even in a system built to disperse it. The longer the confrontation with Washington runs, the more the IRGC moves from being merely the strongest node toward becoming the effective decision-maker .

The IRGC still cannot run the economy, conduct diplomacy and preserve clerical legitimacy all at once. This is why it governs through that coalition rather than in place of it. But a prolonged state of war is exactly the condition under which that necessity begins to erode, because all decisions become related to the conflict and how best to prevail.

The current system in Iran and its position towards a negotiated deal out of the war exists on a spectrum. At one end stand the economic stabilisers around Pezeshkian and Araghchi. Their camp consider the prolonged stalemate untenable and want sanctions relief, the release of frozen assets, and an end to the blockade.

Next come the pragmatic sovereigntists led by Ghalibaf and Rezaei – regime insiders who see diplomacy as the only way out, but not when it comes at the expense of strategic autonomy. Their camp will accept negotiation only from a position of strength and insist that the missile programme and the regional network of proxies stay off the table entirely.

Further along sit the security-first coercionists gathered around Vahidi and the IRGC, who view diplomacy as a tactical instrument at all times subordinate to military leverage.

At the far end are the ideological rejectionists of the Paydari Front and Saeed Jalili’s network. These fundamentalists regard any agreement with Washington as a form of surrender. They function less as a governing bloc than as a spoiler capable of raising the political cost of any deal.

A chance to talk

It is misleading to mistake Iranian dissent for dysfunction, when in truth it is neither. Here is a system arguing with itself about existential questions of statecraft. What is striking about the country now is not the depth of the disagreement but the extent to which the factions agree on the fundamentals.

The spectrum has, without ever announcing it, largely agreed that some form of negotiation is the way out of the crisis. The stabilisers want a deal to rescue the economy. The sovereigntists want one to bank the gains of the war. Even the IRGC appear to want a channel of its own, as recent reports about the Trump administration relaying messages via Iraqi Kurdistan directly to the IRGC leadership suggest.

The fight is therefore no longer about whether to bargain. It’s about the precise ways and means of improving Iran’s position before it commits to anything irreversible.

Washington needs to understand that Iran has already begun to make its choice. Every US economic D-Day that reaches once more for the escalation trap strengthens the rejectionists who insist that confrontation with the US and Israel is permanent. It weakens the factions that have, against considerable odds, talked the system toward the negotiating table.

By seeking to talk to the IRGC, Donald Trump has shown he understands he has a unique opportunity to get out of this self-inflicted quagmire. But he must not allow his ego to stand in the way of the mediators’ arduous efforts.
