stories.title: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
stories.summary: The UK says Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 September 2026, 13:54 BST

Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.

The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.

It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported , external US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina.

The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

Trump's remarks were labelled "nonsense" by Labour MP Dame Emily Thornberry, who chairs the Commons foreign affairs committee, as she asked the UK government to issue an official response in the House of Commons.

Foreign Office Minister Uma Kumaran replied: "The UK has no doubt about its sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.

"They are and will always remain a British overseas territory in line with the wishes of the Falkland islanders.

"The UK is steadfast in our support for the islanders' rights of self-determination."

Kumaran said she had seen Trump's comments, adding: "Our position remains unchanged."

Defence spending pledges

In April, an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters suggested the US was considering options to punish Nato allies it believed had failed to support its war in Iran.

The options reportedly included the prospect of the US reviewing its position on Britain's claim to the Falklands.

Reports of this proposal have re-emerged in recent days in relation to defence spending.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will honour a commitment made by predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to devote 3.5% of UK gross domestic product (GDP) on core defence spending by 2035.

On Tuesday, Chancellor John Healey told The Times , external he would "set out a clear path" to meeting that Nato pledge at the next government spending review, expected in the spring of next year.

He added that this would also include a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP.

Healey resigned as defence secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government following a row over military spending.

His resignation letter in June expressed his frustration that the government had no clear timetable to hit the 3% spending target, which he believed should happen by 2030.

Chagos deal questions

The UK government has also faced questions over whether it will continue with a deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.

It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.

Kumaran told MPs on Tuesday that "maintaining long-term operational control and security of the base remains a top priority and is the entire basis for the UK-Mauritius agreement."

The minister also said funding for the treaty would be provided for "within the existing spending review settlements" for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and the Ministry of Defence.

Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge criticised the remarks and said the deal "belongs on the ash heap of history".

He said in a statement: "Burnham should show some backbone and break with this terrible legacy of the Starmer years by ditching his crazy Chagos deal once and for all, and spending the savings on our armed forces."

In the Commons, Conservative shadow Foreign Office minister Wendy Morton noted Sir Keir's administration acknowledged in April that the Chagos treaty had become "impossible to agree at political level" and asked what had changed.

Kumaran said the Burnham government would "continue to work with the US and Mauritius to find a way forward that is in the UK's best interests and protects our national security".

stories.title: New laws planned to tackle rogue funeral firms
stories.summary: The government plans to regulate undertakers after the jailing of Hull funeral director Robert Bush.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The law change comes after police investigated Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull

Published 5 hours ago

A minister has said the government is working on new laws to "drive rogue operators out of the funeral industry".

Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Yvette Cooper gave a written update to Parliament on proposed legislation to regulate undertakers.

It comes after a Hull funeral home director was jailed last month for failing to bury or cremate people and giving bereaved relatives the ashes of strangers.

Robert Bush was sent to prison for 20 years after he admitted 67 offences, including denying 30 people a decent and proper burial, theft from charities, and fraudulent trading over a period of almost 12 years.

During his sentencing, Hull Crown Court heard that 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes were found by police raiding Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in March 2024.

Bush, 48, of Otley in West Yorkshire, was "preoccupied with his own enrichment", defrauded nearly 200 families out of £562,117 and "caused anguish and pain on a scale beyond comprehension", the judge said.

Cooper said Bush's actions were "utterly abhorrent, and my thoughts remain with all the bereaved families in Hull who were so badly let down."

She said that, as part of the plans, the Law Commission would review the criminal law in relation to the deceased and "consider any gaps in existing legal protections and make recommendations on the creation of new offences, if they are needed".

Cooper said detailed plans and the timetable for their introduction would be announced "in due course".

Robert Bush was jailed at Hull Crown Court for 20 years last month

The funeral industry in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is currently self-regulating, relying on voluntary codes and inspections by trade associations.

Anyone can set up as a funeral director without formal training, registration or oversight.

MPs and families affected by Bush's crimes have been lobbying for change.

Nigel Hotham's uncle, Mark Hotham, died in September 2023 and his body was later found in Bush's funeral parlour.

"It's easier to open a funeral director's than it is to open a sandwich shop – and there's more regulation around sandwich shops than there is funeral directors," he said.

Reform UK's Richard Tice questioned on BBC local radio

Published 7 hours ago

Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice has defended decisions to raise council tax and cut spending at local authorities led by the party in England.

Tice faced questions about the party's record in local government in a round of interviews with BBC radio stations ahead of its annual conference this week.

He was asked why Reform UK-led councils had raised council tax, with presenters suggesting the party had given the impression it would do the opposite.

Tice argued Reform UK councillors had shown they were "financially prudent" and were "doing a good job of getting to grips with wasteful spending".

The BBC interviews focused on Reform UK's policies in local government, where the party gained control of 24 councils following local elections this May and last year.

But they also covered national issues and the role of Nigel Farage, following a difficult summer of questions about a £5m gift received and not declared by Reform UK's leader.

The gift, and the parliamentary investigation into it, attracted more attention than the party would have liked in recent months, distracting from its policy announcements on immigration and welfare.

Asked whether he would be prepared to lead the party, should Farage stand down, Tice insisted "Nigel is going nowhere" and would lead the party into the next general election.

The party's conference in Birmingham this week is an opportunity for Reform UK to regain some political initiative and show it is capable of governing.

The party's conference, Tice said, would be about "the first 100 days of a Reform government".

He said Reform UK would be talking about "hope, optimism, and how to create some growth as we start to rebuild Britain".

Council tax came up several times in the interviews with Tice.

In March this year, Farage pledged that if his party took control of further councils in May's local elections, it would ensure council tax rises in those areas would be lower than in those run by any of the other parties.

Tice said a council tax rise of 9% in Worcestershire , while Reform UK was in minority control of the county council, was the "right and proper thing".

Speaking to BBC Hereford & Worcester, he said: "We had to be honest with people and say the council is effectively bust."

Reform UK lost control of the county council on 14 May, after councillors from the party ousted their own leader before a coalition made up of the Green Party, Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and independents took over.

Other topics in the interviews included spending cuts by Durham County Council , led by Reform UK.

Tice said he "trusted our councillors to make those judgements themselves".

He told BBC Radio Cornwall that more affordable housing was "absolutely vital" in areas like theirs, adding his party would introduce a right-to-buy scheme to help people get on the ladder.

He told BBC Radio Leicester climate change was real, but the government should focus on adapting to it - rather than "arrogantly thinking we can stop it".

BBC Radio Newcastle asked Tice if Reform UK was doing enough to ensure professional standards in local government after resignations, expulsions and suspensions in the north east of England, and he responded that "the most professional thing to do is save money".

Speaking to BBC Radio Solent, Tice said Reform UK was "driving the way the decisions are being made" on the Isle of Wight after winning 19 of 39 seats in May.

stories.title: Burghart becomes Tory deputy leader in major reshuffle
stories.summary: The move completes a shake-up of Kemi Badenoch's top team ahead of the party's conference in October.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Alex Burghart is expected to stand in for Kemi Badenoch when she is not present for PMQs

Published 31 August 2026

Alex Burghart has been appointed deputy leader of the Conservative Party, as part of a major reshuffle that saw Sir Mel Stride and Dame Priti Patel sacked.

Burghart has been a close ally of Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, often helping her prepare for Prime Minister's Question Time and big Commons moments.

His appointment is the final element of Badenoch's substantial shadow cabinet reshuffle, much of which took place on Monday.

In other moves, Andrew Griffith will replace Sir Mel as shadow chancellor, while Tom Tugendhat will take the place of Dame Priti as shadow foreign secretary.

With most polls putting the Conservatives in third place, lagging behind Labour and Reform UK, Badenoch will be hoping a refreshed shadow cabinet will help boost her party's popularity ahead of the party's conference in October.

Burghart is expected to be the go-to stand-in at PMQs, and also deputise for Badenoch when necessary, as well as continuing as Shadow Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and Shadow Northern Ireland Secretary.

He was elected as MP for Brentwood and Ongar in Essex on the same day Badenoch was elected in the nearby constituency now known as North West Essex in 2017.

A senior Conservative source said: "Kemi is changing the way the Conservative Party approaches economic policy and creating a new economic leadership team for the next phase, focused on growth, higher living standards and fiscal credibility."

Badenoch said that as shadow chancellor, Sir Mel had helped the party rebuild economic credibility and become an effective opposition.

Sir Mel, who was appointed to the role following Badenoch's leadership election in 2024, described his time in post as a "great honour".

New shadow chancellor Griffith said the Tories will deliver "an economic revolution" with lower taxes, Britain drilling again to bring energy costs down, slashing red tape and Labour's Employment Rights Act.

"The Conservatives will always back the risk-takers and wealth creators who deliver growth, investment and jobs," he said.

The Tory source described Griffith as a "no-nonsense, pro-growth shadow chancellor with real business experience".

Claire Coutinho, previously the shadow energy secretary, after her maternity leave will replace Griffith as shadow business secretary and act as his deputy.

Opposition parties highlight Andrew Griffith's role in the 2022 Liz Truss mini-Budget

Before he became MP for Arundel and South Downs in 2019, Griffith served as a top executive at Sky and as chairman of Just Eat.

As a Treasury minister, he defended Liz Truss' 2022 mini-Budget .

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson described Griffith as "a key architect of Liz Truss's disastrous mini-Budget" and said the shadow cabinet featured politicians "who hammered family finances and left our public services crumbling".

That message was echoed by other parties. Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: "His appointment to shadow chancellor shows they're happy to forfeit any claim to economic credibility in their race to the bottom with Reform UK."

Reform UK's economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "They haven't changed and still aren't sorry for the damage they inflicted on our country."

Dame Priti, who had been shadow foreign secretary since 2024, will return to the backbenches and will take on a new international role strengthening the Tories relationship with sister parties and centre-right movements abroad.

Badenoch has selected Damian Hinds as the new shadow health and social care secretary after Stuart Andrew confirmed he will be returning to the backbenches .

Katie Lam has been named as the new housing secretary, after Sir James Cleverly quit the front bench, announcing he wants to run for London mayor .

Claire Coutinho will become shadow business secretary after maternity leave

Badenoch's reshuffle is intended to bring solutions to a number of problems.

First, she wants to retire those members of her top team that have had a relatively low profile, or who have not been delivering sufficient blows to both Labour and Reform UK.

Badenoch paid a warm tribute to Sir Mel but some recent polls suggested that Reform UK were more trusted on the economy than the Conservatives.

And that is something Kemi Badenoch felt needed to change.

Second, while familiar faces like Dame Priti were useful to have in the top team as they brought high-level government experience, they might also remind voters of the party they decisively rejected in 2024.

There has been a changing of the old guard, and Badenoch is now focusing on who can take the Conservatives into the next election - faced as she is by a new Labour leader and cabinet.

Third, she wants to focus on issues where Labour is perceived to be vulnerable.

One such area is defence spending and national security.

So as shadow foreign secretary she appointed Tom Tugendhat - a former security minister and current army reservist who served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He will work as part of a team with the shadow defence secretary.

Some opinion polls rate the economy as the most important issue for voters, above asylum and immigration, and again the Tory leader believes the government is vulnerable here, with sluggish growth.

So she has announced a new Conservative economic unit headed by Griffith, with his extensive business experience.

Coutinho as his deputy is seen as a rising Conservative star who has performed well in her previous role shadowing the former energy secretary Ed Miliband in the Commons, and as a potential future chancellor if the Conservatives were ever to recover electorally.

But the Tory leader has also included the former Conservative chairman and City Minister Richard Fuller in the unit, concentrating on fiscal responsibility and tax.

He will be deployed as an attack dog if - as she believes he will – the chancellor raises taxes in the Budget.

But the role will also underline that the Conservative leader is serious about making her sums add up, in contrast to her characterisation of Reform UK's plans as ill-thought out.

The question now though is whether Badenoch will change her own approach to political leadership.

While some of her top team may be seen as lacklustre, how much opportunity did they get to shine?

She tends to make the big announcements and is ubiquitous on the media.

If the Conservatives are to convince voters they are once again a government in waiting then the public will have to see that there is breadth and depth in the team that is shadowing current ministers.

stories.title: As US-Canada tensions flare, who’s calling the shots in Trump’s trade team?
stories.summary: US trade representative Jamieson Greer has a level-headed reputation but commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House adviser Peter Navarro also have key roles Having reportedly read Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, in French, during a military tour of duty in Iraq, Jamieson Greer considered himself an unlikely target for accusations of francophobia. stories.body:
US trade representative Jamieson Greer has a level-headed reputation but commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House adviser Peter Navarro also have key roles

Having reportedly read Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, in French, during a military tour of duty in Iraq, Jamieson Greer considered himself an unlikely target for accusations of francophobia.

But Donald Trump’s US trade representative, hitherto one of the president’s less high-profile cabinet members, found himself in that uncomfortable position amid the acrimonious collapse of bilateral trade talks with Canada that now threatens to degenerate into an all-out trade war between the two close trading partners whose economies are tightly intertwined.

An apparent pending deal between Washington and Ottawa aimed at avoiding damaging tit-for-tat tariffs broke down at the last minute, with Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, claiming his country had come “under attack” from the US.

Among the multiple and complex points of disagreement was a Canadian accusation that US negotiators had pressed for a weakening of legal protections for the French language, which is most heavily spoken in the province of Quebec.

Canadian provisions include legislation that mandates streaming and online video companies to invest in and promote Canadian content and promote the French language. Carney cast US objections to such regulations as a deal-breaker, and said they amounted to “threats to French language and culture”.

For Greer, a fluent French speaker who once served as a Mormon missionary in Belgium, France and Luxembourg, the charge was too much. “I speak French, too,” he told CNBC , dismissing the claims as “a funny, fake story”.

“My kids speak French,” he said. “One of my kids was born in Paris. So I like the Québécois, and I like that they speak French. What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada.”

The controversy may be the closest glimpse the public will see of Greer being rattled. By Thursday, in what was being being seen by some Canadian officials as a potential olive branch, he was peddling a softer line on the language issue.

“President Trump, myself and the US government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada,” he told CBC , the Canadian broadcaster. “We know that this is quite sensitive and quite important, and we actually champion the use of French.”

The impact was undermined hours later, however, when Trump publicly signed a retributive executive order supposedly changing the name of Lake Ontario – one of the Great Lakes which has shores on both countries – to Lake America. Petty as the act was, it seemed to graphically illustrate the limited freedom of manoeuvre held by anyone representing a president so preoccupied with trade.

And Greer is not the only official seeking to steer the president’s aggressive agenda on trade – raising questions over who is really in control.

Moving the goalposts

Those who have met and worked with Greer describe the 46-year-old – who served as a military lawyer in Iraq, where he is reported to have read Hugo’s classic novel between bombardments – as a model of calm and expertise.

“I have high respect for him. He been pretty creative in terms of trying to thread the needle with other countries as he tries to promote Trump’s trade policies,” said Wendy Cutler, a former US trade representative’s negotiator who has met Greer several times. “From a professional viewpoint, he’s extremely impressive. His reputation as being very level-headed, a very calm demeanor, and not someone who loses his temper or who grandstands.”

It is not known if Greer retained his sang-froid in private as the talks with Canada unravelled, just days after Trump himself publicly declared a deal was at hand.

According to reports, the agreement was derailed after Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, objected to the scale of proposed tariffs reductions on imports of Canadian steel, aluminium and cars, sectors falling under his responsibility after Trump declared them areas of national security under the 1962 Trade Expansion Act .

Carney, explaining why Canada decided to abandon the talks, pointed to disunity among the US negotiators. The White House has denied claims of division between Greer and Lutnick, but seasoned commentators are skeptical.

“Lutnick viewed all this as his turf, and here is Greer, who is the designated guy to be effectively the trade minister, if you think about it in the context of other countries, conducting the negotiations,” said William Reinsch, a senior adviser to the Center for Strategic and International Studies and a former undersecretary for commerce. “It appears Greer was willing to go farther than Lutnick was.

“From the Canadian point of view, this was a disagreement that developed late in the day and led the Canadians to believe that the United States was moving the goalposts.”

Cutler, who served Republican and Democratic administrations during a 27-year stint as a US trade negotiator, said tensions within negotiating teams were not unprecedented, but were normally ironed out before talks reached the critical stage.

“I think the challenge under this administration is that you have Greer in charge of the trade portfolio, but Lutnick’s in charge of section 232 investigations [restricting foreign import on national security grounds] and that’s where a lot of the sensitive issues are,” said Cutler, now vice-president of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

after newsletter promotion

‘Trump whisperer’

Greer cut his trade negotiating teeth as chief of staff to Robert Lighthizer, US trade representative in Trump’s first presidency, who played the leading role in renegotiating Washington’s economic ties with Mexico and Canada, and the former North America Free Trade Agreement (Nafta), which was replaced with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) in 2020.

He was chosen for the position when Lighthizer apparently indicated he did not wish to be considered for the post a second time. “Greer plays the same role that Lighthizer played,” said Reinsch, who noted, however, that Greer lacked his former boss’s intimate understanding of Congress.

“He figures out legal ways to do what Trump wants to do, and to get as much of Trump’s objectives accomplished as is possible within the framework that he has to operate in,” added Reinsch. “So that allows him to come back to Trump on occasion and say, ‘there’s a better way to get what you want than what you’ve employed so far.”

Another complicating element may be Peter Navarro, the president’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing.

He is reckoned by analysts to be a “Trump whisperer” on Canada, despite a belief that his influence has been marginalized compared with the first Trump presidency, when it was widely joked, according to Reinsch, that Lighthizer was reluctant to travel outside Washington for fear that Navarro would persuade the president to adopt impractical trade policies in his absence.

Navarro, who went to jail for contempt of Congress after refusing to comply with a subpoena from the committee investigating the 6 January 2021 insurrection, vented in an appearance on the C-Span network last week.

Asked to respond to an article in the Guardian by the Canadian writer Jen Gerson, who wrote that US retaliation should be taken as a warning by other western allies, Navarro said: “Madam, your country screws us. You’re in bed with the Chinese and playing games with us.

“Look in the mirror at your tariffs codes. You are the problem.”

Blame game

Navarro has voiced concern that Canada has allowed the import of nearly 50,000 Chinese-manufactured electric vehicles under a most favoured nation agreement, which he fears will ultimately end up crossing the border to be sold in the US.

“Navarro’s worried that the whole USMCA negotiation is really about how do we prevent Canada and Mexico from being a backdoor to Chinese stuff,” Reinsch said. “He would probably have argued last week that the deal wasn’t any good because it wouldn’t shut down Chinese imports in the United States.”

Yet the focus on Trump’s advisers cannot obscure the president’s own fixation with tariffs. Carney referred to agreements being “signed in pencil”, suggesting that Trump would try to change terms even after the details had been hammered out.

“The larger Canadian objection was not due to interagency American disagreement,” Reinsch said. “Trump has very strong fixed views on trade. He thinks tariffs are good. So if you’re going to blame somebody, don’t blame Lutnick or Greer. Blame Trump, because I’m quite confident he had the last word on this.”

Regardless of where blame is apportioned, the consequences of Carney’s defiance will reverberate beyond Canada, analysts say, as other countries forced to confront Trump’s threats of tariffs reassess and recalibrate how they should respond.

“Other countries are watching the developments with Canada very closely,” said Cutler. “Some of our other trading partners have expressed similar frustrations [to the Canadians] to me privately, and so we could be at a turning point.

“It is possible that what we’re experiencing with Canada now spreads to other countries.”

stories.body:
Rights group claims 300 homes were destroyed in Tibet and number of missing people is ‘far higher’ than Beijing admits

A Tibetan advocacy group says hundreds of homes were destroyed on the Tibetan side of the border in last week’s deadly floods, raising questions about Beijing’s official account of the scale of the disaster.

Public discussion about the flash floods has been restricted, with security officials in Tibet announcing on Sunday that it had penalised at least 10 people for sharing “false disaster information”. There was no further information on the nature of the penalties.

Chinese authorities say 16 people have been confirmed dead and 546 are missing, including 261 foreign citizens. But the International Campaign for Tibet says its sources believe the number of casualties is significantly higher, with at least 300 homes destroyed.

Tencho Gyatso, the president of the campaign group, told the Guardian: “What is visible in Nepal exposes what is being concealed in Tibet. Four villages – Sale, Serchung, Labi and Rizi – were among the hardest hit, with approximately 300 homes reportedly destroyed and many people still missing.”

She said the “little information that we can gather from the ground” suggested the numbers affected were “far higher” than Chinese officials had reported.

On 26 August, the collapse of a glacier triggered deadly floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, destroying entire villages. The death toll on the Nepal side has passed 900, with more than 4,000 missing. Tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada among others remain unaccounted for in the mountainous region that is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

Advocacy groups say there has been a stark contrast in the amount of information presented on either side of the border. Chinese coverage has been dominated by official state media reports , with few unofficial accounts about the scale of the disaster and its aftermath.

Independent verification is extremely difficult in Tibet, where foreign journalists face severe restrictions. Tibetans can face imprisonment for sharing information with journalists and advocacy groups outside China .

Gyatso said: “Officially released glimpses, however important, cannot tell us what is happening across all affected communities.”

Her Tibetan advocacy group said several sources reported that survivors had been moved to Gyirong, which is about 30km (18 miles) from the border crossing that was hit by the flooding. They are said to be under strict management and restricted from communicating freely.

According to a report posted on 27 August on the Tibet Daily, a state-run newspaper, two Tibetans were detained for questioning for posting “rumours” that more than 1,000 people had been swept away close to the border.

Gyatso said: “The Chinese government portrays it like it’s only happening in Nepal and there’s nothing across the border. For any type of crisis, the way China handles it is that there is no crisis. The party is in control.”

Posts relating to the disaster continued to trend on Chinese social media on Monday, with many comments echoing official narratives and supporting rescue efforts.

A Weibo post by Hu Xijin – a prominent Chinese commentator and former chief editor of the state-run Global Times – attracted more than 300 comments and thousands of likes. He accused a small number of voices of seeking to “stir controversy by fabricating baseless claims”.

However, one comment under his post questioned why all the updates were coming from the Nepali side of the border.

On Sunday, Tibetan public security officials said they had penalised people for sharing misleading information or “disrupting online order” with posts about the disaster.

In one case, a user identified only as Zhang disputed the official death toll, posting: “Clearly thousands of people were swept away, yet the authorities reported only three deaths and 265 people missing.”

Another user named Zhou said: “In this wave of mudslides, one entire village was wiped out. It was definitely more than a thousand [deaths].”

Maya Wang of Human Rights Watch said: “The instinct of the Chinese government is always to kind of control and to ensure the narrative which is to portray itself as a very efficient government.

“There have been questions raised over how the development of the valleys in an ecologically fragile and geologically fragile area may have related to this disaster.”

Human rights groups say that Beijing maintains tight controls over movement, religion and information in Tibet. Tibetan groups in exile have long been critical of large-scale development in the region, which they consider geologically fragile.

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said ⁠on Monday that the ⁠release of ⁠information about the floods and mudslide near its ⁠border with Nepal was transparent and timely.

“Malicious smear campaigns ‌and hype using the disaster situation does not align with popular sentiment,” said Guo Jiakun, ‌in response to allegations that China censored videos of the disaster and understated the number of missing people.

When asked about allegations ‌that China ignored warnings from scientists over hydropower construction, he said: “We ⁠firmly oppose such baseless and malicious speculation.”

stories.body:
Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars

For many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, seems superfluous given the grim economic situation in their country.

Iranians are facing runaway food inflation, closed petrol stations and a seemingly never-ending depreciation of the nation’s currency caused by a lack of foreign exchange reserves.

Vegetable oil in Iran in August cost 383% more than a year ago. The price of eggs rose by 294%, chicken by 177% and red meat by 148%.

The cratering economy leaves the country’s political class on edge as they try to prevent economic conditions leading to social chaos.

In truth, long before Donald Trump’s latest sanctions push , Iran’s economy had become a parallel battlefield in which the country’s economic commanders were struggling to maintain control.

On 23 August, the US dollar reached roughly 2m rials on Iran’s open market, a new record.

Three days later, Iran’s statistical centre announced that year-on-year inflation in August reached 84.4%; the rolling annual average rate was about 65%.

As purchasing power in Iran collapses, households are buying fewer goods.

Diets are changing, clothes are being patched up and repaired rather than replaced, and medicine is in short supply, though it can be found on the hidden market.

According to the Mehr news agency, demand for red meat fell by 50% in April 2026 compared with the same period last year. There has also been a leap in the consumption of potatoes, leading to shortages.

Basic goods like eggs are now unaffordable to middle- and working-class families, Golshan Fathi, an Iranian feminist, recently said. “They don’t understand that people can no longer afford even a normal life.”

Mohsen Zavaar, a biomedical engineer, said: “For part of the population, the issue is no longer buying a house or a car; the issue is cutting out meat, reducing food quality, postponing medical treatment, and scraping by until the end of the month.”

Frustrated by the inability of officials to tackle the problems, he added: “The people don’t want miracles – they want decisions.”

The crisis has spread beyond food and clothes. Long lines of cars stretched through parts of Tehran and the north-eastern Iranian city of Mashhad on Tuesday and Wednesday as motorists queued for fuel, with some lines blocking entire streets. Many petrol stations, including some of the largest, were closed.

Officials blamed isolated panic buying caused by rumours of a government-planned price increase, or Israeli bombs that destroyed two of Tehran’s three main oil depots.

Inside the government, anxious discussions have been under way for weeks about increasing the price of oil to reduce costly subsidies, but the political class know from past experience that there could be significant pushback. A sudden overnight petrol price rise of 50% in November 2019 sparked week-long violent protests .

Public anger has been exacerbated by an admission that vested interests in the government made it hard to tackle fuel smuggling.

Saqab Esfahani, deputy to Iran’s president, said: “Both political factions in the country are involved in fuel smuggling, and if I were to shut down their operations, they would break my windows.”

Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been urged to investigate the remarks.

However, transparency over the economic conditions in Iran is likely to decrease.

Fatemeh Mohajerani, a spokesperson for the Iranian government, said recently that future poverty statistics would only be published with the permission of the country’s supreme national security council, making the decline in living standards akin to a classified state secret.

Iran’s leaders now cast the home front as part of the war against America. Hojatoleslam Taeb, the new head of the Basij paramilitary force and a close ally of Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, recently delivered a speech that conjured up an image of resistance against market forces distorted by US sanctions.

As part of this war, he said it was necessary to reduce petrol consumption by as much as 10% to reduce the need for expensive imports. Avoiding unnecessary travel would be an act of patriotism, he implied.

But these patriotic appeals increasingly have an air of desperation as the economic crisis becomes worse.

Mohsen Rezaei, the new, more hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, said: “I advise young people to start producing the products they and society need in their homes, just as they gather in public spaces.”

Mohammad Taheri, editor of the economics magazine Tejarat Farda, said the advice reminded him of Mao’s “backyard steel furnaces” during the Great Leap Forward. Mao encouraged people to produce their own steel, with disastrous effect.

Amirhossein Hashemi-Javid, an energy expert, said Iran’s true economic crisis was its inability to export oil due to the US blockade. “The channels for selling Iranian oil are drying up.

“Oil that cannot reach customers from the well provides no revenue for the Iranian economy; it is simply barrels that incur increasing production, storage and risk costs every day,” he said.

At some point, the Iranian government will have to decide if it might achieve more through diplomacy than through continued confrontation.

Only six months on from starting a war, after Trump promised protesters in January that help was on its way , the only commodity the US is now offering Iranians is deeper poverty.

stories.body:
Outsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solution

T he alarm sounded 16 years ago. In 2010, China blocked exports of key rare earths to Japan in a row over disputed islands in the East China Sea. The critical minerals are essential to everything from advanced weaponry and iPhones to electric vehicle batteries and wind turbines, so the rest of the world took note. But it didn’t take much action. China still accounts for about 70% of rare-earth mining globally and 90% of separation and processing.

Then, last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war – not with its retaliatory tariffs, but the curbing of rare-earth exports. A scramble for new supplies began in earnest. The year-long trade truce is due to expire in November. The price of erbium, an element essential to communications infrastructure, has already jumped because of fears that export controls will soon be renewed.

The 17 metals known as rare earths are far from rare ; their name refers to the low concentrations in which they are found. Extraction and processing are costly, complex and often dirty, while returns are low. That’s why the US – which dominated the industry in the 1980s – and others outsourced production to China. Any plan to diversify supply chains must somehow build in predictable demand and pricing to succeed. Even now, US rare earths are reportedly flowing to Asia because of the lack of domestic demand. While “Big shovel” is becoming the new driver of geopolitics, rare earths are a tiny slice of the critical minerals market – worth less than $6bn globally last year.

Efforts to diversify supply chains had already begun. But the US-China standoff accelerated them. Last autumn, the Pentagon became the single largest investor in the US firm MP Minerals. In February, the Trump administration announced that it would spend $12bn to create a critical minerals reserve , focusing initially on rare earths. US officials have reportedly described their plan to create new supply chains as a “Manhattan Project” for rare earths. Others question the strategy behind the splurge of money and projects.

China, which imports rare earths for processing and has seen them affected by the war in Myanmar, also wants to diversify its supplies. Washington and Beijing are looking to South Africa, Greenland and, in particular, Brazil , raising grave concern about the ecological impact . Innovation, particularly in finding ways to recycle rare earths or extract them from mining waste or runoff, could help meet demand and reduce environmental damage. But it will not stop the extraction drive.

Earlier this year, the US launched a critical minerals coalition with 54 partners, including Australia, the European Commission and the UK. A multilateral approach is essential. But Europe and others know it would be extremely risky to count on Washington solely, given the unreliability of the Trump administration, its wild use of trade weapons and its threats to invade Greenland. Stockpiles of essential rare earths, serious investment and stronger partnerships with likeminded allies will be central to a solution. The 2025 European Critical Raw Materials Act set targets for reducing import dependence by 2030. France is already home to the biggest facility outside China to process all 17 rare earths, and a deal for Brazilian minerals is under discussion . But many fear that European countries are moving too slowly . That must change.

stories.title: Burnham says Brexit brought ‘decade of low growth’ in first Commons address as prime minister – as it happened
stories.summary: This liveblog is now closed. Read the Guardian’s report of today’s political news here My colleague Richard Partington , the Guardian’s senior economics correspondent, grew up, like Andy Burnham, in the Warrington suburb of Culcheth. He has been home to find out what people there are saying about the new PM. Yesterday, Kemi Badenoch announced a reshuffle, replacing Mel Stride with Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor and Priti Patel with Tom Tugendhat as shadow foreign secretary. Continue reading...
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Early evening summary

Andy Burnham has declared his government can make “this next decade better than the last” in a confident and relatively non-partisan address to MPs. Speaking in parliament for the first time since becoming PM more than six weeks ago, Burnham gave a wide-ranging opening statement and then took questions from more than three hours. Burnham said:

double quotation mark When I stood outside Downing Street six weeks ago, I said Britain needs a circuit breaker after a decade of turbulence, negativity, point scoring and divisive politics. This is what I have outlined today. A clear, coherent, and credible approach to growth that can unlock a feeling of positivity and possibility in every postcode in Britain. Our job in here is to make it real by taking a place first rather than party first approach. It starts with reasserting basic standards for Britain, that this is a country where no one sleeps rough and no community is blighted by an illegal waste tip. And from there, working together to build a new sense of optimism around the country. We can make this next decade better than the last. We can lift the prospects of all our people and places.

Burnham repeatedly made a point of stressing his desire to collaborate with opposition parties, as part of his commitment to doing politics in a new way. He was relaxed and good-humoured and, although he faced criticism from some opposition MPs, he was generally given a fair hearing. He did not have any surprise new announcements, and much of what he said repeated arguments had made over the summer. On many issues he indicated that final decisions have yet to be taken. With the statement still running after three hours and 20 minutes, Burnham is still on his feet.

Keir Starmer is to quit as the MP for Holborn and St Pancras, saying it is the right time for him to leave the Commons.

John Swinney insisted he still planned to introduce a legally binding price cap on bread, milk and other essential food items in Scotland despite fierce opposition from farming and business groups.

After Burnham had been taking questions for two and a half hour, Jeremy Corbyn told him the session had lasted “ longer than the longest World Cup match”. He asked if Burnham would back rent controls.

Burnham said he thought he and Corbyn took part in longer hustings debates during the 2015 Labour leadership contest. On housing, he said “ a package of measures to turn the housing market around” was needed.

Julian Lewis (Con) told Burnham he thought the local government reorganisation amounted to “ shameless gerrymandering”. Lewis represents New Forest East, and he said his constituency was being “torn apart” with part that looks towards the New Forest being taken over by Southampton.

Burnham said he would ask the community secretary to look at this.

Burnham says he is 'concerned' about plans for Freeview TV to be switched off by 2034

David Mundell (Con) asked Burnham if he would review plans for terrestial Freeview TV to be switched off in 2034. This decision would affect a lot of elderly people in rural areas, he said.

Burnham replied:

double quotation mark I am concerned about those plans. I know some of my constituents in Makerfield rely on Freeview. There is perhaps an opportunity to look at this as part of the BBC’s BBC charter renewal process. I can’t give [Mundell] a final answer today, but I recognise it’s a genuine issue that he’s raised. I know it will be of concern to his constituents and let me have a proper look at it.

In response to a question from Labour’s Marsha De Cordova about Europe, Burnham said the next UK-EU summit might take place “the month after next” (ie, in November), but this was still being finalised.

In response to a question from Ellie Chowns , the parliamentary leader of the Green party , Burnham said that he was committed to a carbon neutral future and he was willing to work with the Greens on this.

Burnham says his Northern Ireland border poll comment 'misunderstood', and Good Friday agreement could allow one

Chris Law (SNP) criticised Burnham for ruling out a Northern Ireland border poll on his recent visit to Belfast.

Burnham said Law had “misunderstood” what Burnham was saying. He said he was ruling out a border poll now. He said he was “very aware of every word in the Good Friday agreement”, which says there should be a border poll if there is clear majority support for one, and he said he would “stick to it 100%”.

He also said he cared about Northern Ireland and visited it often.

Burnham suggests Shropshire could also get devolution benefits without being part of combined authority

Helen Morgan , the Lib Dem MP for North Shropshire , said there are no immediate plans for Shropshire to have a combined authority or mayoral authority. People there were worried this would mean they would lose out under Burnham’s devolution plans, she said.

Burnham said he thought devolution deals would only work with unitary local government. He went on:

double quotation mark I don’t think it will work with a two-tier system, but that’s why I said to colleagues in Cornwall, I’m quite happy to see if a deal can be done for a single unitary authority. [See 5.02pm .] That is what I understand members of parliament for Cornwall want working with the leader of Cornwall council. If that is the settled view, I’m not going to try and impose something else. Let’s work with that. And the same could be true in Shropshire, but it needs to be effective and functional and be able to stand on its own two feet.

Burnham urges Scottish government to back bringing Glasgow's bus service back under public control

Zubir Ahmed (Lab) asked Burnham if he could do anything to improve the bus service in Glasgow.

Burnham said he had been surprised to learn how expensive bus fares were in Glasgow. He said he thought there were moves to put the buses under public control in the city, but he had been told the Scottish government was not in favour. He said he hoped they would adopt that approach.

He went on:

double quotation mark A great city like Glasgow should have public transport under its own control. And what I see in Scotland, there is something of the same problem as England, where the capital city has a public transport system that is way beyond what anywhere else has.

Burnham says he has 'open mind' about beefing up elections bill with caps on political donations

Labour’s Stella Creasy said Reform UK has raised £9m in donations this year, with £8m coming from just three UK-based donors. She went on:

double quotation mark Chequebooks are already circling the next general election, and if we wish to defend our democracy and make sure that all voices can be heard equally, we need to make sure it’s not money that talks.

She urged Burnham to accept amendments to the representation of the people bill that would put caps on how much individuals and companies can donate to political parties.

Burnham said that bill as drafted (which only caps the amount that can be given by donors living abroad) was just a start. He went on:

double quotation mark I don’t think anyone on the front bench is saying it’s the end of this matter. We do need to go further. I would encourage [Creasy] to engage with the Defending Democracy taskforce. And certainly I have an open mind about what those further measures might be.

Burnham says he '100%' backs getting social media companies to remove non-consensual explict content more quickly

Wera Hobhouse (Lib Dem) asked about women secretly being filmed on nights out. She said:

double quotation mark In many towns and cities across the country, women are secretly filmed on a night out and the videos are posted online with vile, degrading, misogynistic contents and comments. And the women only find out once these videos have been shared 100,000 times and more, and they do not know what to do and we need to change something. Will the prime minister support the campaign to end this vile practice, including looking at reform to make misogyny a hate crime?

Burnham said, as the father of two daughters, this issue was very much at the forefront of his mind. He said he had recently met Georgia Harrison, who was doing “amazing” campaigning in this area.

He said Harrison wanted social media companies to remove non-consensual explicit content immediately, not just within 48 hours, which is the current deadline. A 48-hour deadline was “totally unsatisfactory”, Burnham said. He said he would support changing that “100%”.

Burnham says E1 settlement on West Bank could kill off prospects for two-state solution for Israel and Palestine

Debbie Abrahams (Lab) asked Burnham would he would do to stop the building of illegal settlements on the West Bank .

Burnham said the plans for the E1 settlement were particularly worrying. They would “lead to decisions being made before the Israeli election which, as I understand it, could imperil, if not end, the two-state solution”.

He went on:

double quotation mark So these matters are urgent. They do need to be confronted. And I believe we will be updating the house soon on those matters. [See 3.04pm .]

Burnham tells Reform UK's Richard Tice he's wrong to think it's either/or with fossil fuels and renewables

Richard Tice , the Reform UK deputy leader, asked when the government would approve the applications for the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields in the North Sea. He repeated his claim about the rush to net zero being “stupid”.

Burnham said Tice needed a better grasp of the facts. He explained:

double quotation mark In Greater Manchester it costs £30 to charge a bus with electric charge, £200 plus to fill a tank of diesel. He really does need to look into the facts a little bit more before he makes statements like that in this house. Solar panels on people’s homes can bring down the cost of their energy and it. And, yes, we need to be pragmatic. We will still need to rely on oil and gas for some years to come. The mistake [Tice] is making is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.

stories.body:
Yield on 30-year gilts highest since 1998 as rout triggered by global factors underlines tricky backdrop John Healey faces

Business live – latest updates

The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be almost halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists into the autumn, economists say.

The UK’s long-term borrowing costs jumped to their highest level since early 1998 on Tuesday as investors dumped government bonds, betting on higher inflation.

The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 30-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hit 5.89% at one point as London markets caught up with a sell-off that swept Japan and the US on Monday, a bank holiday in the UK.

Ten-year gilt yields were around 5.25%, their highest level since the 2008 global financial crisis.

Higher yields progressively increase the cost of financing the government’s debt. If sustained, these would pass through to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)’s forecasts for John Healey’s 28 October budget.

Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, Sanjay Raja, said that based on Tuesday’s yields, Healey’s headroom against the current budget rule would fall from £26bn at Rachel Reeves’s spring forecast to £13.8bn before covering any additional spending plans.

Almost all of the deterioration results from higher government interest costs. The OBR’s March forecast had gilt yields at 5.1% for this year. Gilt yields eased back a bit later on Tuesday – to 5.85% for the 30-year and 5.21% for the 10-year – but they are still well above the predicted level.

Raja suggested Healey would be likely to try to maintain headroom of at least £10bn to assuage market concerns about the government’s commitment to balancing the books. “£10bn to me is the floor. In a perfect world you would want to keep 15,” he said.

In addition to global forces, Raja said higher-than-expected growth in the UK in the first half of the year had also contributed to rising yields. “There are some good reasons,” he said.

The current budget rule is the promise that the government will match day-to-day spending with receipts and only borrow for longer-term projects.

Tuesday’s market moves underline the tricky global backdrop facing Andy Burnham’s government as he returns to Westminster promising to help consumers with the cost of living.

The OBR takes market expectations of future gilt yields during a two-week reference period in to account in its forecasts. It does not announce these dates in advance, but Raja suggested judging by the timing in previous years, the current tumultuous period may be included in its budget projections.

The bond sell-off was driven primarily by international factors. Japanese 10-year yields hit their highest level since the 1990s over expectations that the Bank of Japan would have to raise interest rates to control inflation.

after newsletter promotion

Investors also appeared to be responding partly to higher oil prices, which were up 3.8% at nearly $94 a barrel after renewed hostilities between the US and Iran. Higher energy costs drive up inflation, potentially forcing central banks to respond.

As well as fretting about future price rises, bond investors also appear to be concerned about runaway deficits in the US, where the Trump administration has cut taxes and is having to hand back much of the revenue from swingeing trade tariffs.

The chief economist at the consultancy Capital Economics , Neil Shearing, said: “It’s been a perfect storm for the bond markets: we’ve had these fiscal concerns that have pushed up the long end of the curve, and now that’s being compounded by upward energy price pressure, pushing up interest rate expectations in the short term – and if you’re sitting in the Treasury, none of that is good news.”

Finance ministers and central bankers from the G20 major economies concluded their meeting in North Carolina to discuss the state of the global economy on Tuesday.

The US and Japan took the rare step of intervening jointly in global foreign exchange markets in August in an attempt to prop up the yen, but the Japanese currency subsequently resumed its slide.

Expectations of higher interest rates were also piqued by a speech on Friday by the Federal Reserve chair , Kevin Warsh, in which he said the US central bank would still have “work to do” if inflation did not return to target.

Before Warsh’s intervention, markets were betting on about a one-third probability of an increase in US rates in September, but that has risen to 70%.

Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to rename Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes, to Lake America

Published 31 August 2026

US President Donald Trump has asked tech firm Apple to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America on its Maps platform to comply with his executive order changing the name of the Great Lake, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has said.

Burgum told Fox Business' Mornings with Maria programme on Monday that "the president has reached out to Apple directly", adding: "I'm sure we may be seeing that change coming up soon."

Google made the switch for its US-based users over the weekend, though users in Canada still see the lake, which borders the province of Ontario and the state of New York, as Lake Ontario.

The BBC has contacted Apple for comment.

Canada installs large Lake Ontario sign in latest jab at US Published 2 days ago

The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts Published 1 day ago

The renaming has faced pushback in Canada, where one electrical utility company apologised on Sunday for its map displaying the Lake America name.

Hydro One, a utility company based in Toronto, said in a post on X that the name appeared due to their use of a third-party mapping service.

"We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference," the company said in its statement. "We regret the error and apologise for any confusion it has caused."

Maps by other Ontario-based agencies also appeared to briefly display the name Lake America, including Hydro Ottawa and the Liquor Board of Ontario.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: "He's losing it" - Americans react to Lake Ontario name change

Trump signed the executive order on Thursday seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, following the collapse of trade negotiations between Canada and the US.

The order directs Burgum to "take all appropriate actions" to rename the lake, including updating the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official US government map database.

Google said in a statement on Saturday that its maps will display the Lake America name for US users to comply with the GNIS.

It added that those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. In the rest of the world, users will see the name displayed as: Lake Ontario (Lake America).

Not all map providers are changing the name. MapQuest, an American free web mapping service launched in 1996, said "we're not changing it" in a short Facebook post on Friday.

The platform also unveiled a tool that allows users to change the lake to any name they choose and share their creations.

After its announcement that it will not be changing the name of Lake Ontario, MapQuest rose to the top of the most-downloaded free applications as of Monday morning on the Apple App Store in Canada.

Microsoft, meanwhile, had no comment when approached about its plans for Bing Maps by BBC.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign by the lakeshore on Saturday that read "Lake Ontario Now and Always" in both English and French, Canada's official languages.

"No one's going to call it Lake of America," Ford told American TV host George Stephanopoulos on Sunday. "It's been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It's going to continue being Lake Ontario."

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words.

As with its approach to Hormuz, the US has mistaken applying pressure for an actual strategy. But Tehran has chips of its own to play

D onald Trump has found a new way to promise victory over Iran. After months of war have failed to force Iran’s capitulation or collapse, his administration has unveiled what the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, calls Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to cut it off from what remains of the global economy and threaten foreign governments, banks and companies with sanctions if they continue doing business with Tehran.

There is no question that Iran is vulnerable. Its economy has been battered by years of sanctions, war and a months-long US naval blockade. Iranian officials acknowledge that oil exports and access to foreign currency have been severely constrained. Ordinary Iranians are already enduring high inflation, currency depreciation and worsening living standards. Further economic strangulation will inflict significant additional hardship.

Iran also wants an end to the war. Its president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has said it should seek peace while it can still negotiate from a position of “power and dignity”. But Iran needing a deal is not the same as Iran preparing to surrender. That distinction has repeatedly eluded Trump in formulating his Iran policy: ramping up pressure is not the same as having a strategy. Iran gets a move too.

Indeed, Iranian officials increasingly suggest this strategy has the opposite effect than what was intended. Each successive escalation, in their telling, demonstrates why Iran relinquishing its remaining leverage would simply leave it vulnerable to the next round of US pressure. The emerging strategy therefore appears to combine bargaining with endurance: seek an agreement while demonstrating that it can withstand the pressure without capitulating or abandoning its core terms.

This is why recent Iranian rhetoric deserves more attention than it has received.

Mohsen Rezaei, the new head of Iran’s supreme national security council, has called participation in Washington’s economic campaign an “act of war”. He says Tehran will first try to persuade neighbouring states not to participate, but has threatened their interests if they do. He has even warned that Iran could prevent Gulf oil exports through routes designed to bypass Hormuz.

These statements should not simply be dismissed as declarations of defiance for an audience in Iran. They reflect a consistent strategic logic: Iran cannot defeat the US economically, but it can try to make the economic strangulation of Iran prohibitively expensive for Washington and the countries it needs to enforce it.

That could mean tightening pressure on Hormuz, threatening infrastructure that enables alternative oil-export routes or putting greater pressure on US interests across the region. None of this would help ordinary Iranians. Escalation would compound their suffering. But that is precisely why Washington should think beyond the first-order effects of its own actions.

There is another weakness in Trump’s plan. For Bessent’s threat to work, Washington must persuade or coerce much of the world into participating, especially China, the principal buyer of Iranian oil. Yet Beijing is moving in the opposite direction. It has ordered firms not to comply with US sanctions targeting Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, while its top court recently highlighted a ruling penalising a Singaporean company for complying with US sanctions. Beijing has now warned it will take “all necessary measures” if Chinese interests are targeted.

Washington therefore faces an uncomfortable choice: tolerate continued trade between Iran and China, its neighbours and other partners, or dramatically escalate coercion of the governments, banks and companies that keep those channels open. That risks multiplying the US’s economic confrontations at a moment when it needs international cooperation to isolate Tehran. Bessent acknowledged the danger when asked why Washington was not immediately imposing its most sweeping secondary sanctions. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he responded. That is quite an admission for an operation advertised as “economic D-day” .

With the midterms approaching, the White House has strong incentives to avoid another major escalation that could further disrupt Gulf energy flows and send fuel prices soaring. Tehran knows this. Its gamble is that it can endure and reroute enough commerce while imposing enough costs that Washington and its partners eventually prefer a settlement to continued confrontation.

That makes this a dangerous contest of endurance. Washington is betting Iran’s economy completely breaks first. Tehran is betting the US’s tolerance for the war and its mounting economic costs breaks first.

This has been the recurring flaw in Trump’s approach. In 2018, he left the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, in an attempt to secure more favourable terms. Iran instead expanded its nuclear programme. Military conflict was supposed to force Tehran to accept US terms. Instead, the war expanded and Hormuz became a central source of Iranian leverage. Now intensified economic strangulation is supposed to accomplish what military power could not.

Unless Trump starts thinking several moves ahead, his latest attempt to force Iran into submission could leave the US with even higher energy prices, an even more confrontational adversary and yet another escalation it never counted on.

Total of 804 confirmed dead and more than 3,000 missing amid threat of fresh inundation

‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospital

Rescuers in Nepal and Tibet have battled through leg-sucking mud amid the threat of fresh flooding to search for thousands of people still missing after a deadly wall of water swept through the Himalayan border zone, engulfing entire villages.

The latest updates on Sunday put the number of missing at 3,048, including hundreds of foreigners. There was a total of 804 confirmed deaths across Nepal and Tibet, and reports of some bodies swept downstream possibly as far as India.

Nepal said it had begun the task of burying some of the hundreds of bodies after first taking DNA samples so that families could later reclaim them after identification and perform traditional funeral rites.

The disaster, which struck the border on Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse which sent a wall of water and debris downstream, the US Geological Survey said.

Nepal’s foreign minister called for a global response to the climate crisis, saying the small, poor Himalayan nation was bearing a disproportionate share of its impact.

“Despite having only 0.1% contribution to global emissions, people of Nepal have become major victims of climate change,” Shisir Khanal said on Saturday.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Nepal said on Sunday that 2,502 people, including 592 foreigners, were out of contact in the country. It reported an updated death toll of 788 people.

Chinese authorities on Sunday reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, of whom 261 were foreign nationals, including 104 from Nepal, 49 from India, 33 from Latvia, 18 from the US and 15 British citizens.

In a breakthrough at the weekend, Nepal’s army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site, where more than 100 workers are believed to be trapped.

The home minister, Sudan Gurung, said: “We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside.”

It is a race to reach the workers, who may still be alive inside the tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites. They are among 933 hydropower workers who are among the missing, according to Nepal’s disaster authority.

Nepal warned on Sunday of rising flood waters and urged rescue teams to exercise caution. “We have received information that the flood flow in the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa has increased further,” the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.

Flood warnings were sent to people’s phones early on Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas hit by the floods.

In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some people began returning to ruined homes to see what could be salvaged. Residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they had received since the initial floods.

One resident, Govind Shreshta, told the Associated Press: “Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain. It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mum. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”

The government estimated Nepal’s reconstruction bill could run to billions of dollars.

Officials in Nepal called for forensic testing kits to identify bodies and freezer units to store them in, saying bodies that had been in water could decompose at a faster rate.

Survivors face an agonising wait to learn the fate of missing relatives and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing. “All the settlements near the river were swept away,” Buddhi Ram Dangol told Agence France-Presse in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. “There is nothing left.”

In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, rescue operations were paused at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of more flooding from a newly formed lake. A total of 2,141 rescuers were near the Gyirong site, the Xinhua state news agency reported, including more than 500 in the worst-hit area.

In Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, relatives and friends gathered outside the main government hospital from early morning, desperately searching for news of missing loved ones.

Many shuffled between the help desk and the hospital noticeboard, clutching photographs and scanning lists of patients in the hope of finding them.

Dil Maya Lama stood weeping near the help desk at the hospital, searching for information about her 26-year-old brother, a driver for a hydropower company in Rasuwa. She had travelled from Ramechhap, about 80 miles (130km) away.

“I came here with the hope that I might find him,” she told the Associated Press. “There is no information about him.”

Nelza Moktan sought information about her missing cousin, who also worked as a driver in Rasuwa. “I feel hopeless. It has already been four days,” she said.

stories.title: Business groups urge Swinney to scrap 'ineffective' food price cap plan
stories.summary: More than 20 organisations have written a joint letter to John Swinney urging him to scrap his plan for a legal cap on some food and drink prices.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
John Swinney pledged to put a cap on the price of "essential items" in an SNP election manifesto pledge

Published 31 August 2026

The Scottish government's proposed food price cap will be "ineffective", business groups have told the first minister.

Twenty-three organisations have written a joint letter to John Swinney - who will set out his programme for government on Tuesday - urging him to scrap his plan for a legal cap on some food and drink prices.

Signatories include groups representing retail, food and drink production, manufacturing and distribution businesses in Scotland.

In the SNP's election manifesto it pledged to compel large supermarkets to limit the cost of essential items - such as milk, eggs, cheese and rice - to ease the cost of living.

Swinney's 100-day push gives way to bigger battles ahead Published 2 days ago

How much should we be prepared to pay for our food? Published 29 June

Swinney said people were struggling to afford a basic shop and he had a "public health responsibility" to provide an affordable nutritious diet.

But the joint letter said a statutory cap would not address the "root causes of elevated food prices" - rising production, refrigeration, and distribution costs.

It is signed by groups including the Scottish Retail Consortium (SRC), the Food and Drink Federation Scotland, Scottish Bakers and Dairy UK.

Ewan MacDonald-Russell, deputy head of the SRC, told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme the plans were an "appallingly terrible idea".

"Price caps don't tackle food price inflation," he said.

"They are not a solution, they are a gimmick that sounds quite effective, but it just displaces cost elsewhere.

"We can't see a single example of where this has worked."

MacDonald-Russell pointed to Hungary, where he said a price cap policy led to shortages on the shelves, domestic products being replaced by "cheap imports" and tension between retailers and customers.

The SRC said the policy also risked forcing small shops which are not covered by the proposed legislation to be uncompetitive.

"Scottish consumers benefit from the most affordable food prices in western Europe," MacDonald-Russell added.

"We know food price inflation is a problem, but the best model to deal with it is the one we have right now and price caps are going to make that worse.

"It is giving a false promise that it is going to be able to help with something.

"In reality, there is as good a chance it is going to make the overall cost of a shopping basket higher, because the cost of the scheme as well as the cap have to be absorbed by businesses."

It is thought the proposals would require changes to the UK Internal Markets Act of 2020 , which was brought in after Brexit to prevent trade barriers and regulatory divergence between England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland as powers returned from the EU.

The Scottish government said helping people with the cost of living was a "top priority".

A spokesperson added: "Ministers have welcomed engagement with stakeholders, including retailers, food producers and farmers on proposals for food price controls.

"A consultation will launch shortly for further views."

By proposing a food price cap, John Swinney wants to demonstrate a commitment to tackling the rising cost of living.

In turn that means those who oppose him risk appearing to be on the wrong side of the argument.

There are of course big questions about whether a cap would actually work in practice and if legislation could even get that far.

Firstly, law making takes time. Swinney himself has talked about a year-long process.

Secondly, the Scottish government would probably need the UK government to grant its proposals an exemption from the internal market act which is designed to harmonise the terms of trade across the UK.

UK ministers have not said whether or not they would oblige.

Thirdly, if legislation was eventually approved at Holyrood it would be open to the supermarkets to challenge it in court.

These complications help to explain why this is not the only avenue being explored by the Scottish government.

They have called a "summit" with food producers and retailers next week to consider the way forward.
